name: Sleep mask
lead: A sleep mask, also called an eyeshade or sleeping blindfold, is a covering worn over the eyes to keep light out and make it easier to fall and stay asleep [2]. Wikipedia lists use as a sleep aid, especially during air travel and for people who sleep by day, among the applications of blindfolds generally [1].

Common designs include flat cloth masks in materials such as silk, satin or microfibre, contoured masks with moulded eye cups, weighted masks and gel masks that can be warmed or cooled [2]. Sleep masks are distinct from cosmetic under-eye masks or patches, which are skincare products rather than light blockers [2].

In looksmaxxing communities a mask is treated as a cheap, portable alternative to darkening a room, in support of sleep quality and, indirectly, appearance. Published evidence is strongest in hospital settings, where masks have usually been tested together with earplugs; trials in healthy home sleepers with appearance outcomes were not found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: General consumer product; light-therapy masks for retinal disease are a separate research category [4]

paras: Flat masks are usually a fabric pad with an elastic strap. Contoured designs use foam cups or a moulded shape that leaves space in front of the eyelids, which manufacturers describe as avoiding pressure on the eyes and letting the wearer blink without touching fabric [2]. Weighted masks add gentle pressure, and gel masks can be heated or chilled [2]. Adjustable straps and materials such as mulberry silk are common features in retail descriptions [2].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, separates these light-blocking masks from skincare eye masks, which are hydrogel, fabric or gel patches applied to the skin for puffiness or dark circles and usually not worn for light exclusion [2].

Blindfolds of cloth have long been used for many purposes, from games to symbolism, and Wikipedia describes use as a sleep mask as one application [1]. Grokipedia states that dedicated sleep masks are a relatively modern accessory with little documented ancient history, and associates their wider use with industrial artificial lighting and later with air travel and growing interest in sleep hygiene [2]. These historical statements come from an AI-generated source and have not been independently verified.

A mask reduces the light reaching the eyes in a bright environment. The proposed rationale is that blocking light avoids arousals caused by light and avoids suppression of melatonin, a hormone linked to the circadian sleep-wake cycle, and so supports sleep onset and continuity [2]. Light can also reach the retina through closed eyelids, and research has examined this deliberately: a study of pulsing blue light delivered through closed eyelids looked at acute melatonin suppression and phase shifting in dim-light melatonin onset [9].

Most trials come from intensive care. Systematic reviews have pooled studies of eye masks and earplugs for sleep promotion in critically ill patients [7][8]. A 2024 randomized trial of 128 surgical intensive care patients compared an ergonomically designed sleep mask with a control arm given earplugs and an eye mask; the ergonomic-mask group reported higher sleep quality on the Richards-Campbell questionnaire (about 50.9 versus 37.6, Cohen's d reported as 0.450) and lower discomfort scores [5]. Because the control group also used a mask, the trial compares mask designs rather than mask versus nothing.

A 2026 randomized, controlled, crossover home study of 91 adults with mild sleep difficulties tested a gently vibrating sleep mask against a control mask across three 14-night periods, tracking sleep with a validated noncontact device [6]. The abstract excerpt available does not report the outcome figures.

Several trials involve masks that emit light rather than block it. A 1997 controlled study from the University of California, San Diego examined nocturnal light delivered by a lit sleep mask or bedside lamp on menstrual cycle length; cycle lengths shortened at 235 to 250 lux but not significantly more than at under 1 lux, and the authors said spontaneous remission or suggestion could not be excluded [3]. The CLEOPATRA phase 3 trial randomized 308 adults with early diabetic macular oedema to an organic light-emitting sleep mask or a sham mask for 24 months [4], and an earlier safety study evaluated the same type of device in healthy volunteers and patients [10]. These concern a retinal therapy and not ordinary light-blocking masks.
No randomized trial found in the sources reviewed tests a light-blocking sleep mask against skin appearance, wrinkles or other cosmetic outcomes.

Reported downsides are mild: pressure or irritation, skin reactions to materials, discomfort from wearing something on the face, and the need to wash masks regularly. A case report described mask-like chorioretinal atrophy in a child with Alagille syndrome; its title refers to a pattern resembling a sleep mask rather than damage from wearing one [11].

Within looksmaxxing, masks are discussed as the portable counterpart to blackout curtains, useful when travelling or when a room cannot be darkened. Claims about appearance depend on the link between sleep quality and skin or facial features, which the sources reviewed do not test directly. Smart masks with sensors for eye movement or breathing have also been prototyped in engineering studies [12][13].

Retail guidance emphasises fit around the nose, strap adjustability, whether the mask applies pressure to the eyelids, breathability of the fabric, and washability [2]. Prices typically range from about $10 to $30.
